claims.text: A machine-learning-driven predictive model integrated with detailed thermal-processing data can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
As-cast or conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs exhibit multiphase microstructures.
Such Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni microstructures contain both desired and undesired phases.
A data-driven model can design optimized annealing and controlled-cooling schedules that tune phase transformations.
Controlled temperature–time profiles and cooling rates can reliably trigger targeted phase transformations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
An appropriate processing atmosphere is required to reliably trigger the targeted phase transformations.
Optimized thermal processing controls the formation and distribution of phases and precipitates, including coherent strengthening domains.
The ML model integrates processing parameters and microstructural-characterization data.
Integrating these data allows the model to decode complex phase-transformation kinetics.
The model predicts thermal profiles that promote desirable phase assemblages and suppress unwanted transformations.
The predicted thermal profiles control phase selection by adjusting nucleation and growth rates.
ML-guided treatment produces a more homogeneous microstructure with controlled precipitate size and distribution.
The resulting microstructure improves mechanical and functional properties relative to conventional heat treatments.
Conventional thermal processing adjusts only global thermal profiles.
Conventional thermal processing often produces coarse, inhomogeneous phase distributions.
The success of the ML approach depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of its training data.
The model may be less predictive when novel or unforeseen transformation pathways occur.
Quantitative phase-kinetics predictions and generalization across processing conditions remain uncertain.
A controlled comparison of identically initialized samples subjected to conventional and ML-recommended treatments can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in phase homogeneity, target-phase fraction, or mechanical properties would falsify the hypothesis.
